title: The State of Model Routing — NVIDIA, Cognition, OpenRouter

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 52%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The discussion is fundamentally about building infrastructure and tools for developers who create multi-model agent systems. OpenRouter is a developer platform, Cognition builds Devin as a developer tool, and NVIDIA provides NeMo, Dynamo, and Flex Run for developers building routing systems.

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: Cognition's Devin is a coding agent, and much of the discussion centers on coding workflows: sub-agent codebase exploration, terminal bench results, feature request to debugging session evolution, and Fusion's application to coding tasks. The panel explicitly notes Fusion is not yet well optimized for coding but that is a primary use case.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: Model routing is a cross-domain concern applicable beyond coding. The panel discusses classification tasks, deep research, heartbeat-driven workloads, and the general principle of routing in-distribution easy tasks to small models across any application domain.

summary: This panel on model routing features Nader Khalil (NVIDIA, moderator), Walden Yan (Cognition), Alex Atallah (OpenRouter), Carter Abdallah (NVIDIA), and Tanay Varshney (NVIDIA). The discussion explores how multi-model systems route tasks across models of varying cost and capability. Walden describes Cognition's Fusion router, which keeps a frontier model for planning and hard decisions while delegating implementation to cheaper models, achieving a 40% cost reduction for Devin's intelligence level. He argues that naive task-based routing is fragile for agentic workloads because sessions evolve mid-session, requiring a frontier model as a supervising watcher. Cognition's sidekick architecture replaces sub-agents with a single continuous running context that keeps the KV cache warm, making cached tokens roughly 10x cheaper. Alex reveals OpenRouter's auto router sat nearly unused for two years until OpenClaw's ten-minute heartbeats created one app with two completely different intelligence needs, sparking broader routing adoption. The panel debates whether compaction is primarily for intelligence (preserving model quality) rather than cost, as model performance degrades sharply well before advertised million-token context windows—200K tokens is a practical ceiling. Self-hosting is presented as a way to bypass API providers' 5-minute cache eviction windows and enable workload-specific optimization. Tanay introduces hallucination probes—internal model state analysis using linear probes and perplexity—as a proxy for detecting when a model is lost. The panel closes debating whether routing is a product or infrastructure, with Alex arguing that even a future single dominant model would need delegation for caching, and noting that Opus tops OpenRouter's classification spending despite opportunities for small-model routing on in-distribution tasks.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent framework for understanding multi-model agent systems in production. The software engineering concepts (sidekick architecture, KV cache warmth, self-hosting economics, API gateway routing) describe the infrastructure patterns that make multi-model routing feasible and cost-effective. The AI concepts (frontier model delegation, jagged capabilities, out-of-distribution detection, hallucination probes) describe the intelligence layer that determines which model handles which task and when to escalate. The bridge between these layers is the economics: cache miss penalties (10x), token efficiency scaling with intelligence, and the fundamental insight that compaction is an intelligence optimization rather than a cost optimization. Together, they explain why naive routing fails (jagged capabilities and evolving session complexity), what replaces it (frontier-model-as-watcher with sidekick architecture), and how the economics evolve (self-hosting for custom cache durations, market-spend-based auto routing, and model co-design). The panel's closing question—whether routing is product or plumbing—connects the engineering patterns to industry structure, with web infrastructure's centralization trajectory providing a historical analogy.
temporalContext: The video was published in early August 2026 (run manifest: Aug 6; web verification: Aug 9), during a period of rapid developments in model routing. OpenRouter launched a major Auto Router update on Aug 10, 2026, and announced joining Stripe on Aug 19, 2026—a significant ownership change 13 days after the panel. NVIDIA published the NeMo Switchyard developer blog on Aug 11, 2026. Fortune published an industry overview on Aug 9, 2026. The panel reflects the state of model routing as multi-model architectures transitioned from research to production deployment, with key products (Cognition's Fusion, OpenRouter's auto router, NVIDIA's NeMo Switchyard) all reaching maturity simultaneously.
takeaways: Cognition's Fusion router cuts Fable-level intelligence cost by 40% by keeping a frontier model for planning while delegating implementation to cheaper models.
Small models pushed out of their training distribution thrash in tool-call loops, potentially costing more than a frontier model; on terminal bench, Opus scores 3x better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku.
Cognition uses a sidekick architecture instead of sub-agents: one continuous running context keeps the KV cache warm, making cached tokens roughly 10x cheaper and allowing role swapping.

OpenRouter's auto router sat nearly unused for two years until OpenClaw heartbeats every ten minutes created one app with two completely different intelligence needs, sparking broader routing adoption.

Compaction is primarily for intelligence, not cost: it forces a cache miss costing 10x more, and model quality falls off a cliff well before advertised million-token windows—200K tokens is a practical ceiling.
Self-hosting transforms cache economics: organizations can set custom cache durations and optimize for specific workload shapes rather than accepting API providers' amortized general-use pricing.
Hallucination probes analyzing internal model states (linear probes, perplexity) offer a proxy for detecting when a model is lost, potentially more informative than token-count heuristics.

Prompts are not portable across model architectures; they are domain-specific and part of the agent-building process, with errors best diagnosed by smart models rather than mechanical tuning frameworks.
Even a future single dominant model would need delegation for caching benefits, since the orchestrator retains more context and models have limited memory.
On OpenRouter's public data, Opus is the top model by dollar spent on classification tasks, indicating large and growing opportunities for routing in-distribution easy tasks to small models.

concepts.name: Model Routing
concepts.explanation: The practice of selecting appropriate models for different tasks based on cost, capability, and workload profile, ranging from naive task-type-based routing to sophisticated multi-model orchestration with frontier-model-as-watcher patterns.
concepts.importance: Central theme of the panel; model routing is emerging as a critical infrastructure layer as multi-model systems become production standard.

concepts.name: Frontier Model Delegation
concepts.explanation: Architecture where a frontier model handles planning and hard decisions while delegating implementation to cheaper models, achieving 40% cost reduction in Cognition's Fusion router.
concepts.importance: Core design pattern for cost-effective multi-model agents; demonstrates that frontier models need not handle every token to maintain quality.

concepts.name: Jagged Capabilities
concepts.explanation: The observation that models have uneven strengths across sub-domains, requiring intimate understanding of each model's capabilities for effective routing. Complementary model techniques can yield up to 10% higher accuracy on benchmarks.
concepts.importance: Fundamental motivation for routing: no single model dominates across all sub-tasks, making model selection a non-trivial optimization problem.

concepts.name: Out-of-distribution Detection and Thrashing
concepts.explanation: Small models pushed outside their training distribution thrash in tool-call loops, potentially costing more than a frontier model. On terminal bench, Opus scores 3x better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku on out-of-distribution tasks.
concepts.importance: Defines the failure mode that routing must prevent; detecting out-of-distribution operation is a critical safety and cost concern.

concepts.name: Fusion Router
concepts.explanation: Cognition's multi-model routing architecture that keeps a frontier model for planning while delegating implementation to cheaper models, reducing intelligence-level cost by 40%.
concepts.importance: Production-deployed routing system demonstrating real-world cost-quality tradeoffs in a coding agent context.

concepts.name: KV Cache Eviction and GPU Memory Limits
concepts.explanation: At inference time, GPU memory limits how many caches can stay loaded; unused caches get offloaded after approximately 5 minutes, imposing operational constraints on routing and context management.
concepts.importance: Physical hardware constraint that shapes all caching and routing decisions; self-hosting with more memory or unified memory systems offers flexibility.

concepts.name: Hallucination Probes
concepts.explanation: Internal model state analysis using linear probes, perplexity analysis, and magnitude analysis to estimate how lost a model is in its thinking, offering a proxy for when a model needs escalation beyond simple token-count heuristics.
concepts.importance: Provides a more informative signal for routing escalation decisions than token-count thresholds, potentially enabling automatic detection of model confusion.

concepts.name: Model Co-design with Orchestration Systems
concepts.explanation: Training models alongside orchestration systems, experimenting with RL training for both orchestrator and executor roles, blurring the line between router and model. The next big step according to Walden.
concepts.importance: Represents the frontier of routing research: models trained to collaborate naturally may reduce the need for external routing logic.

concepts.name: Pareto-optimal Model Selection
concepts.explanation: OpenRouter's approach of providing Pareto-optimal models for coding tasks given a tunable cost threshold, selecting the best model on the cost-quality frontier.
concepts.importance: Operationalizes the cost-quality tradeoff as a configurable parameter, enabling users to choose their position on the Pareto frontier.

concepts.name: Token Efficiency Scaling with Intelligence
concepts.explanation: Smarter models are more token-efficient with tools, making multi-model systems scale better with intelligence—a non-obuitive property that favors frontier-model-as-orchestrator designs.
concepts.importance: Counterintuitive insight that intelligence and cost efficiency are not always in tension; smarter models can be cheaper at the system level.

concepts.name: Heartbeat-driven Routing
concepts.explanation: Workload profile from periodic heartbeat requests (e.g., OpenClaw's 10-minute heartbeats) creating one app with two completely different intelligence needs, which drove OpenRouter's auto router adoption after two years of disuse.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how novel workload patterns create routing needs that did not previously exist, explaining the sudden adoption of previously unused routing infrastructure.

concepts.name: Lossy vs Non-lossy Context Management
concepts.explanation: Analogy to human memory: lossy context is effective because non-lossy systems like file systems serve as fallbacks. A good harness should have everything it needs to find what it needs even if not everything is immediately in context.
concepts.importance: Provides a design philosophy for agent context management: embrace lossy compression in working memory while maintaining lossy fallbacks in external systems.

concepts.name: RL Training for Model Collaboration
concepts.explanation: Cognition is training models to be good collaborators, experimenting with training both orchestrator and executor roles through reinforcement learning, so frontier models become naturally collaborative.
concepts.importance: Suggests routing may eventually be internalized through training rather than imposed externally, changing the long-term architecture of multi-model systems.

concepts.name: Compaction as Intelligence Optimization
concepts.explanation: Compaction is primarily for intelligence preservation, not cost reduction: model quality falls off a cliff well before advertised million-token windows, with 200K tokens as a practical ceiling. Compaction is useful when taking a cache miss anyway during model routing.
concepts.importance: Reframes a commonly misunderstood tradeoff; many practitioners assume compaction saves cost when it actually incurs a 10x cache miss penalty primarily to preserve intelligence.

concepts.name: Auto Router (Market-spend-based Selection)
concepts.explanation: OpenRouter's auto router uses aggregate market spend data to select models automatically, which sat nearly unused for two years before heartbeat-driven workloads created adoption. On public data, Opus tops classification spending despite small-model opportunities.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates both the potential and the adoption challenge of automated routing; market signals can drive model selection but require the right workload patterns to unlock value.

concepts.name: In-distribution vs Out-of-distribution Task Routing
concepts.explanation: In-distribution tasks suit small models while out-of-distribution tasks require frontier models to avoid thrashing. Opus scores 3x better than Haiku on terminal bench at 1/10 the cost despite Haiku being cheaper per token.
concepts.importance: Core principle for routing decisions: task-model fit matters more than per-token cost when evaluating total cost of ownership.

concepts.name: Router as Product vs Plumbing
concepts.explanation: The closing debate on whether routing will be a standalone product or infrastructure plumbing, with Tanay drawing an analogy to web infrastructure where routing controls centralized over time, and Alex arguing even a future dominant model needs delegation for caching.
concepts.importance: Strategic question that determines whether routing remains a differentiable capability or commoditizes into infrastructure.

concepts.name: Flex Run and Dynamic Model Footprints
concepts.explanation: NVIDIA's Flex Run technology distills a main model into smaller footprints and switches decoding based on task complexity, enabling dynamic model size selection within a single deployment.
concepts.importance: Represents an alternative to inter-model routing: intra-model routing through distilled footprints that share architectural lineage.

concepts.name: Sidekick Architecture
concepts.explanation: Cognition's pattern of replacing sub-agents with a single continuous running context that keeps the KV cache warm, making cached tokens roughly 10x cheaper and enabling role swapping between orchestrator and executor.
concepts.importance: Replaces the common sub-agent spawning pattern with a more cache-efficient architecture, directly addressing the cost penalty of cache misses in multi-model agent systems.

concepts.name: KV Cache Warmth and Cache Hit Rate Management
concepts.explanation: The practice of maintaining a warm KV cache through continuous context to avoid cache misses that cost roughly 10x more for input tokens. Cache eviction is driven by GPU memory constraints, with typical API provider eviction windows of 5 minutes.
concepts.importance: Cache economics fundamentally shape routing and compaction decisions; a single cache miss can erase the savings from using a cheaper model.

concepts.name: Context Compaction as an Engineering Tradeoff
concepts.explanation: Compressing context to preserve model intelligence rather than reduce cost. Compaction forces a cache miss costing 10x more, and model quality falls off a cliff well before advertised million-token windows—200K tokens is a practical ceiling, under 100K if possible.
concepts.importance: Challenges the common assumption that compaction is a cost optimization; understanding this tradeoff is critical for designing effective agent context management strategies.

concepts.name: Self-hosting for Cache Duration Control
concepts.explanation: Self-hosting bypasses API providers' 5-minute cache eviction windows, allowing organizations to set custom cache durations based on business logic and optimize for specific workload shapes (e.g., 32K average cache vs 64K).
concepts.importance: Transforms cache economics for organizations with predictable workloads, offering significant cost advantages over amortized API provider pricing.

concepts.name: API Gateway Provider Routing
concepts.explanation: OpenRouter's two-layer routing architecture: model routing (which model answers) and provider routing (which provider serves that model), with inverse-square price weighting, automatic failover, and session stickiness.
concepts.importance: Represents a production-scale routing platform pattern where routing is decomposed into independent layers, enabling market-spend-based model selection and provider-level failover.

concepts.name: Prompt Portability Across Model Architectures
concepts.explanation: Prompts are not portable across model architectures; they are deeply domain-specific and part of the startup building process. Value accrues from discovered doom loops and recovery strategies specific to each model.
concepts.importance: Constrains the design space for routing systems: prompt rewriting or adaptation is needed when switching models, complicating naive model substitution.

concepts.name: Sub-agent Spawning for Parallel Codebase Exploration
concepts.explanation: Pattern where multiple cheaper agents explore a codebase more comprehensively within the budget a single frontier model would consume, trading per-token cost for broader coverage.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that cheaper models can outperform frontier models on specific tasks when given more token budget, challenging the assumption that frontier models are always superior.

concepts.name: Direct Compute Capacity vs Per-Token Pricing
concepts.explanation: Cognition's early strategy of buying direct compute capacity from providers instead of paying per-token, recognizing that cached token economics were far cheaper before API providers introduced cache pricing.
concepts.importance: Illustrates how infrastructure procurement decisions are driven by cache economics, and how the API pricing landscape has evolved to accommodate caching.

concepts.name: Prompt Tuning via Model Intelligence
concepts.explanation: Walden's approach of using smart models to diagnose prompt failures rather than mechanical gradient-descent-style tuning frameworks: telling a smart model what decision was made and asking it to diagnose errors, then having agents update and regression-test.
concepts.importance: Offers a heavier-weight but more trustworthy alternative to automated prompt optimization, leveraging model reasoning over mechanical search.

concepts.name: Workload-Specific Cache Optimization
concepts.explanation: Tailoring cache durations and configurations to specific workload profiles (e.g., heartbeat-driven workloads vs reasoning workloads vs agent loops) rather than accepting API providers' amortized general-use pricing.
concepts.importance: Different workload profiles create distinct caching and routing needs; understanding workload shape is essential for cost-effective multi-model deployment.

sections.title: Welcome and the multimodel premise
sections.summary: Nader Khalil introduces the panel on model routing, noting NVIDIA's belief in a multi-model world and the release of NeMo Triton models with full customization recipes.

sections.title: Panel introductions
sections.summary: Walden Yan (Cognition) introduces Devin and customer deployment questions about model ROI. Carter Abdallah (NVIDIA) discusses cost challenges of frontier models. Tanay Varshley (NVIDIA) describes his work on model evaluations and router design.

sections.title: How Devin Fusion beats the frontier models
sections.summary: Walden explains Fusion reduces Fable-level intelligence cost by 40% by keeping the frontier model for planning and delegating implementation to cheaper models. Smarter models get better at delegating work.

sections.title: Let the frontier model plan and delegate the work
sections.summary: Cheaper implementation models can use more tokens within the same budget, spinning off multiple sub-agents for deeper codebase exploration. The trade-off is both more cost-efficient and more comprehensive.

sections.title: Jagged capabilities: no one model wins everything
sections.summary: Tanay emphasizes models have jagged capabilities across sub-domains. Routing requires intimate understanding of each model's strengths. Complementary model techniques can yield up to 10% higher accuracy on benchmarks. Alex Atallah arrives from OpenRouter.

sections.title: Why naive task based routing is fragile
sections.summary: Walden argues naive task-based routing is extremely fragile for agentic tasks because sessions evolve from questions to feature requests to debugging. The solution is keeping a frontier model as a watcher that detects when delegated agents are out of their depth.

sections.title: Sharing context without paying for it twice
sections.summary: Walden explains most context goes to one model by default, with compacted summaries of file readings and high-level thinking passed back to the main agent. Context compaction is applied to routing to avoid redundant token costs across multiple models.

sections.title: Should the orchestrator be the big or the small model
sections.summary: Alex raises the internal debate on whether the outer orchestrator model should be big or small. A big-model orchestrator benefits from caching for price savings. He emphasizes in-distribution versus out-of-distribution tasks, citing terminal bench where Opus scores 3x better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku.

sections.title: In distribution versus out of distribution
sections.summary: Alex notes OpenRouter's deep research results used the smart model as the outer wrapper. Walden counters that caching benefits can also apply to the side agent, introducing Cognition's sidekick architecture: one continuous running context instead of sub-agents, keeping KV cache warm at 10x cheaper cached tokens.

sections.title: Training models to collaborate
sections.summary: Walden discusses RL training for models to collaborate, experimenting with training both orchestrator and executor roles. He argues co-designing models with orchestration systems is the next big step. Tanay connects this to NVIDIA's post-training for harnesses that include routing.

sections.title: Flex Run and flexible model sizes
sections.summary: Tanay describes NVIDIA's Flex Run technology, which distills a main model into smaller footprints and switches decoding based on task complexity. He raises the question of lossy compaction versus lossless representations like ASTs for preserving agent state.

sections.title: Lossy context and the systems you fall back to
sections.summary: Tanay draws an analogy to human memory—lossy but effective—arguing agents can rely on non-lossy systems like file systems as fallbacks. A good harness should have everything it needs to find what it needs even if not everything is immediately in context. Walden adds that smarter models are more token-efficient with tools, making multi-model systems scale better with intelligence, which is not obvious.

sections.title: How a heartbeat created the auto router
sections.summary: Alex explains OpenRouter's auto router sat nearly unused for two years until OpenClaw began sending heartbeats every ten minutes, creating one popular app with two completely different intelligence needs. OpenRouter now offers Pareto code (Pareto-optimal model for coding tasks with a tunable threshold), fusion (orchestrating multiple models), and plans for more routing primitives. He notes OpenRouter cannot see into KV caches unless running models themselves but passes through cache-hit savings to users. Nader observes a perfect storm for routing: performance gains from planning, workload profile changes with agents and reasoning, and heartbeat-driven token generation each create distinct routing needs.

sections.title: Routing between local and cloud
sections.summary: Carter raises local-versus-cloud routing for privacy (detecting sensitive prompts for on-device processing) and cost savings (maximizing DGX Spark utilization when paying only for power, not cloud tokens). NVIDIA is working on hybrid local-cloud routing as an emerging sector.

sections.title: Compaction versus routing
sections.summary: Walden argues compaction alone does not solve cost or throughput problems because intelligence and cost differentials between models are so large. Compacting forces a cache miss costing 10x more for input tokens. The main reason to compact is intelligence: model quality falls off a cliff well before advertised million-token windows, with 200K tokens as a practical ceiling and under 100K if possible. Compaction is useful when taking a cache miss anyway during model routing.

sections.title: How a small model signals it is out of its depth
sections.summary: Alex asks whether small models generating lots of tokens is a signal to switch to a larger model. Walden explains detection mechanisms, noting that small models often cannot self-detect when they need help—sometimes the big model must detect it. Cache refresh cadence (e.g., 5-minute cache lifetimes) also plays a role in switching decisions.

sections.title: Cache duration and self-hosting economics
sections.summary: The 5-minute cache refresh is a practical operational constraint: at inference time, GPU memory limits how many caches can stay loaded, and unused caches get offloaded. Self-hosting bypasses this limit, allowing custom cache durations based on business logic. Tanay notes dynamic cache durations depend on deployment hardware—GPUs with more memory or unified memory systems like Rubin offer more flexibility. Self-hosting also enables workload-specific optimization (e.g., 32K cache vs 64K cache) instead of accepting API providers' amortized general-use pricing. NVIDIA offers Dynamo with pre-fixed cache optimizations for self-hosters.

sections.title: Cognition's early compute strategy
sections.summary: Walden reveals that when Cognition started building agents in 2024, no API providers offered cached token pricing, so sending the same 100K tokens repeatedly meant paying full price. Cognition solved this by buying direct compute capacity from providers and paying for underlying compute rather than per-token, recognizing cached token economics were far cheaper. He envisions future systems backing caches to storage like S3 for longer retention.

sections.title: Hallucination probes and model state detection
sections.summary: Walden notes Cognition has not yet explored token-count as a switching signal empirically. Tanay describes hallucination probes that analyze internal model states—magnitude analysis, linear probes, perplexity—to estimate how lost a model is in its thinking. Since cache prefill is just vectors, classifiers can be tuned to guesstimate various model states, offering a proxy for when a model needs help beyond simple token-count heuristics.

sections.title: Prompt portability across models
sections.summary: Nader asks how non-portable prompts affect routing across different model architectures. Walden argues prompts are deeply domain-specific—part of the startup building process—with value accruing from discovered doom loops and recovery strategies. Alex envisions tuning OpenRouter's fusion against real production data, using signals like user-initiated model upgrades or system-detected misrouted tasks as a feedback loop for an auto-research system that continuously reiterates on routing.

sections.title: Prompt tuning approaches
sections.summary: Walden expresses skepticism toward mechanical gradient-descent-style prompt tuning frameworks, preferring to leverage model intelligence: telling a smart model what decision was made and asking it to diagnose why it went wrong, citing specific prompts, then having agents update and regression-test. He trusts this heavier-weight system more than low-level mechanical optimization.

sections.title: Is the router a product or plumbing
sections.summary: Nader asks whether routing will be a standalone product or part of plumbing, noting that on DGX Spark, collaborative multi-agent spawning maximizes compute utilization on edge hardware. Tanay draws an analogy to web infrastructure, where routing controls centralized over time. Walden sees frontier models becoming naturally collaborative through training. Alex argues that even a future single dominant model would still need delegation for caching, since the orchestrator retains more context and models have limited memory. He notes that on OpenRouter's public data, Opus is the top model by dollar spent on classification tasks, underscoring large and growing opportunities for routing in-distribution easy tasks to small models. Nader closes the panel with thanks and applause.

organization.name: Cognition
organization.summary: Cognition is an applied AI lab that builds Devin, the first autonomous AI software engineer. Headquartered in San Francisco with offices in New York and Austin, Cognition is funded by Founders Fund, Lux, 8VC, and Bain Capital Ventures, with approximately 343 employees and total funding of approximately $1.6 billion. The company's run-rate revenue reached $492M as of May 2026. In this panel, co-founder and CPO Walden Yan presented Cognition's Fusion router architecture for Devin, which keeps a frontier model as planner while delegating implementation to cheaper models, achieving a 40% cost reduction for Fable-level intelligence. Cognition also uses the sidekick architecture with continuous running context instead of sub-agents to keep KV cache warm at roughly 10x cheaper cached tokens, and originally bought direct compute capacity from providers before API providers offered cached token pricing.
organization.status: Active independent company; Devin Desktop launched, Series D funding announced May 2026, $492M run-rate revenue

Route AI Agents Across Models with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard

technologies.label: Multi-Model Routing
technologies.summary: Model routing is the central architectural pattern discussed by all three panelist organizations. The practice of selecting and orchestrating multiple models of varying cost and capability for different parts of an agent workflow. Three production implementations are presented: Cognition's Fusion router (frontier model for planning, cheaper models for implementation, 40% cost reduction), OpenRouter's Auto Router (market-spend-based model selection that sat unused for ~2 years before heartbeat-driven adoption), and NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard (open-source routing library with tuning-free and tunable routers). Key principles include jagged capabilities (no single model wins all sub-tasks), the fragility of naive task-based routing for agentic sessions that evolve mid-session, the distinction between in-distribution tasks (suit small models) and out-of-distribution tasks (require frontier models to avoid thrashing), Pareto-optimal model selection with tunable cost thresholds, heartbeat-driven workloads creating new routing needs, model co-design with orchestration systems via RL training, and the constraint that prompts are not portable across model architectures. The panel closes debating whether routing is a standalone product or infrastructure plumbing, with Tanay drawing an analogy to web infrastructure where routing controls centralize over time.
technologies.role: Central theme of the panel; Cognition, OpenRouter, and NVIDIA each present their routing systems and debate principles including jagged capabilities, in/out-of-distribution routing, Pareto-optimal selection, and whether routing is a product or plumbing.

technologies.label: KV Cache Economics and Management
technologies.summary: KV cache economics fundamentally shape routing and context management decisions in multi-model agent systems. Cached tokens cost roughly 10x less than non-cached tokens, but cache eviction is driven by GPU memory constraints with typical API provider eviction windows of 5 minutes. A single cache miss can erase savings from using a cheaper model. Cognition's sidekick architecture addresses this by maintaining one continuous running context instead of spawning sub-agents, keeping the KV cache warm and enabling role swapping. Self-hosting transforms cache economics by allowing custom cache durations based on business logic and workload-specific optimization rather than accepting API providers' amortized general-use pricing. NVIDIA's Flex Run technology distills a main model into smaller footprints and switches decoding based on task complexity, offering an intra-model alternative to inter-model routing. Cognition's early strategy of buying direct compute capacity rather than paying per-token illustrates how infrastructure procurement decisions are driven by cache economics before API providers introduced cache pricing.
technologies.role: Major subtopic; Walden explains the sidekick architecture for KV cache warmth, Tanay discusses cache eviction windows and self-hosting economics, and Cognition's direct compute capacity strategy is revealed as an early workaround before API cache pricing existed.

technologies.label: Context Compaction for Intelligence
technologies.summary: Context compaction is presented as primarily an intelligence optimization rather than a cost optimization. Compaction forces a cache miss costing roughly 10x more for input tokens, so it is not a cost-saving measure. The main reason to compact is intelligence: model quality falls off a cliff well before advertised million-token context windows, with 200K tokens as a practical ceiling and under 100K if possible. Compaction is most useful when taking a cache miss anyway during model routing. The design philosophy draws an analogy to human memory: lossy context is effective because non-lossy systems like file systems serve as fallbacks, and a good harness should have everything it needs to find what it needs even if not everything is immediately in context. No specific named implementation of compaction was discussed; it is described as a technique applied within Cognition's agent architecture and broadly applicable to multi-model systems.
technologies.role: Significant discussion point; Walden argues compaction is primarily for intelligence not cost, with model quality falling off a cliff well before advertised context windows. Tanay draws the lossy human memory analogy with file-system fallbacks, and notes that smarter models are more token-efficient with tools, making multi-model systems scale better with intelligence.

technologies.label: Model State Detection via Hallucination Probes
technologies.summary: Hallucination probes analyze internal model states to detect when a model is lost in its thinking, offering a more informative signal for routing escalation decisions than simple token-count heuristics. Techniques include magnitude analysis, linear probes trained on hidden layer activations, and perplexity analysis. Since cache prefill produces vectors that can be classified, these probes can be tuned to guesstimate various model states, potentially enabling automatic detection of when a small model needs escalation to a frontier model. This is presented as a research direction, with Walden noting Cognition has not yet explored token-count as a switching signal empirically, and Tanay describing the probe-based approach as an alternative to mechanical heuristics.
technologies.role: Brief but notable discussion; Tanay describes hallucination probes using linear probes, perplexity, and magnitude analysis as a proxy for detecting when a model is lost in its thinking. Walden notes Cognition has not yet explored token-count as a switching signal empirically.

outcomes: Understand why naive task-based routing fails for agentic sessions with evolving complexity and why a frontier-model-as-watcher pattern is needed
Learn how delegation from a frontier planner to cheaper implementation models reduces cost while maintaining quality, achieving 40% cost reduction in Cognition's Fusion router

Recognize that in-distribution tasks suit small models while out-of-distribution tasks require frontier models to avoid thrashing, with Opus scoring 3x better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku on terminal bench
Understand the sidekick architecture's advantage over sub-agents for KV cache warmth and cost efficiency, making cached tokens roughly 10x cheaper
Learn about co-designing models with orchestration systems and RL training for collaboration, blurring the line between router and model
Understand that compaction is primarily an intelligence optimization, not a cost optimization, because compacting forces a cache miss costing 10x more
Recognize how workload profiles such as heartbeats, reasoning traces, and agent loops create distinct routing needs that drove OpenRouter auto router adoption after two years of disuse
Learn about local-cloud hybrid routing for privacy preservation and hardware utilization optimization on edge devices like NVIDIA DGX Spark
Understand self-hosting economics for cache duration control and workload-specific optimization beyond API providers' 5-minute eviction windows
Recognize hallucination probes using internal model states such as linear probes and perplexity analysis as a method for detecting model state and informing routing escalation decisions
Understand why prompts are not portable across model architectures and require domain-specific empirical tuning informed by discovered failure modes
Learn about production-data-driven routing optimization using user behavior signals like model upgrades as a feedback loop for auto-research systems
Understand that even a future single dominant model would need delegation for caching, since the orchestrator retains more context and models have limited memory

Build a sidekick architecture with continuous context and measure KV cache hit rates and token costs compared to a naive sub-agent spawning approach
Implement an escalation router that detects when a cheaper model is thrashing in tool-call loops using token-count signals and hallucination probes, comparing detection accuracy

Analyze cache economics: given a 5-minute API eviction window and 10x cache cost ratio, calculate break-even points for self-hosting vs API for different workload profiles including heartbeat-driven workloads

Design a local-cloud hybrid routing policy that detects sensitive prompts for on-device processing while maximizing edge hardware utilization, justifying routing decisions with privacy and cost tradeoffs
